newsitem.title: GERMANY: Volkswagen earnings soar, Volvo disappoints.
newsitem.headline: Volkswagen earnings soar, Volvo disappoints.

text.p: Europe's largest automaker, Volkswagen AG, Wednesday reported a 56 percent leap in pre-tax profits for the first nine months of the year, while Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo posted weaker-than-expected earnings.

Volkswagen said pre-tax profit rose to 1.48 billion marks ($971 million), between January and September, up from 948 million ($624 million), a year ago. Group sales climbed 14.2 percent to a record 74.5 billion marks ($49 billion).
Volkswagen said it was heading for higher full-year sales and earnings.
"We expect better profit and sales than the year before," a Volkswagen spokesman said.
After-tax profit climbed to 465 million marks ($305 million) from 185 million marks ($122 million) for the same period in 1995.
"The Volkswagen figures are good figures, especially when you consider the gathering difficulties of other companies in the sector," said John Lawson, auto analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.
The automaker has surpassed its own expectations for much of this year, winning European market share by fighting to keep costs and prices down, analysts said.

"This confirms VW as one of the winners in the sector. VW has shown excellent growth rates in terms of sales ... and it is one of the fastest-growing car companies in the current situation," Lawson said.
Volkswagen said car production rose 8.7 percent during the first nine months to 2,741,914 units, while worldwide deliveries to customers climbed 12.6 percent to 2,986,977 units.

Sweden's Volvo reported a 12 percent rise in pre-tax profit, but the higher earnings came after a 7.8 billion crown ($1.2 billion), capital gain on the sale of a stake in U.S./Swedish drugs group Pharmacia & Upjohn.
Volvo said its profits rose to 12.03 billion crowns ($1.83 billion), but sales fell 12 percent to 113.6 billion crowns ($17.3 billion). The profits fell short of industry expectations.
Operating profit plunged to 2.32 billion crowns ($353 million) from 8.84 billion ($1.34 billion).
Industry analysts said they were disappointed by a below par performance by Volvo's American truck operation.
"Lower sales, depressed prices and higher production and product development costs were the main reasons for the decline," chief executive Soren Gyll said in a statement.
Volvo Truck's performance was a major handicap, suffering from weak demand in North and South America, although European deliveries rose 6 percent.
Volvo's Car division showed a 70 percent drop in operating income to 573 million crowns ($87 million).
